item.title: “Monks, I have searched for the gratification of form. Whatever gratification there is in form — I have found it. To what extent there is…
item.description:
“Monks, I have searched for the gratification of form. Whatever gratification there is in form — I have found it. To what extent there is gratification in form — that I have seen well with wisdom. Monks, I have searched for the peril of form. Whatever peril there is in form — I have found it. To what extent there is peril in form — that I have seen well with wisdom. Monks, I have searched for the escape from form. Whatever escape there is from form — I have found it. To what extent there is escape from form — that I have seen well with wisdom. Monks, I have searched for the gratification of feeling … of perception … of formations … of consciousness. Whatever gratification there is in consciousness — I have found it. To what extent there is gratification in consciousness — that I have seen well with wisdom. Monks, I have searched for the peril of consciousness … the escape from consciousness … That I have seen well with wisdom. Monks, as long as I did not directly know as it actually is the gratification as gratification, the peril as peril, the escape as escape in regard to these five aggregates of clinging, I did not declare that … ascetics, brahmins, devas, and humans. But when I directly knew them, then the knowledge and vision arose in me: ‘My mind is liberated, imperturbable. This is my last life, now there is no further becoming.’”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.27

item.title: “Monks, an untaught ordinary person might become disenchanted, dispassionate, and liberated regarding this body composed of the four great elements. Why is that? Because he…
item.description:
“Monks, an untaught ordinary person might become disenchanted, dispassionate, and liberated regarding this body composed of the four great elements. Why is that? Because he sees this body composed of the four great elements increasing and decreasing, being taken up and discarded. Therefore, an untaught ordinary person might become disenchanted, dispassionate, and liberated regarding it. But regarding that which is called mind, intellect, consciousness — here, an untaught ordinary person is not capable of disenchantment, not capable of dispassion, not capable of liberation. Why is that? For a long time, monks, an untaught ordinary person has been attached, regarded as ‘mine,’ grasped at: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self.’ Therefore, he is not capable of disenchantment, dispassion, or liberation regarding it.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.61

item.title: “Monks, what is Right Mindfulness? Monks, here a monk abides contemplating the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having restrained covetousness and sorrow…
item.description:
“Monks, what is Right Mindfulness? Monks, here a monk abides contemplating the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having restrained covetousness and sorrow in the world; abides contemplating feelings as feelings … mind as mind … phenomena as phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having restrained covetousness and sorrow in the world. This, monks, is called Right Mindfulness.”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 22 – Mahāsatipaṭṭhānasutta

item.title: Sitting down to one side, that monk said to the Venerable Sāriputta: “Venerable Sāriputta, a monk who is my companion has abandoned the training and…
item.description:
Sitting down to one side, that monk said to the Venerable Sāriputta: “Venerable Sāriputta, a monk who is my companion has abandoned the training and returned to the lower life.” - “That comes to be, friend, for one who does not guard the sense faculties, does not know moderation in eating, and is not committed to wakefulness. For such a person, it is impossible that he would continue the perfectly pure holy life for his whole life. Friend, a monk who does guard the sense faculties, knows moderation in eating, and is committed to wakefulness — it is possible that he would continue the perfectly pure holy life for his whole life. Therefore, friend, you should train thus: ‘We will guard the sense faculties, know moderation in eating, and be committed to wakefulness.’ Thus, friend, you should train.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.120

item.title: “Those who day and night Devote themselves to the teaching Of the Perfectly Enlightened One — They calm the fire of greed By always perceiving…
item.description:
“Those who day and night
Devote themselves to the teaching
Of the Perfectly Enlightened One —
They calm the fire of greed
By always perceiving the foul.

With the mind of loving-kindness, the supreme,
They calm the fire of hatred.
With the fire of delusion,
By wisdom they extinguish it —
Wisdom that leads to penetration.

Ardent, mindful,
Day and night they calm
These fires without remainder —
They make them cease without remainder.

Those noble ones who have seen,
The wise with knowledge,
Having rightly known the destruction of birth,
Do not go to renewed existence.”

From: Itivuttaka 93
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā: “How tiresome are sensual desires! Impure, foul, full of thorns — Seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, Renunciation is firmly secure. I…
item.description:
Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā:

“How tiresome are sensual desires!
Impure, foul, full of thorns —
Seeing the danger in sensual pleasures,
Renunciation is firmly secure.
I went forth from Rājagaha,
Leaving home for homelessness.”

I know my former lives,
The divine eye is purified.
I know the minds of others,
The ear-element is purified.

I have attained psychic powers,
The destruction of defilements is attained.
I have attained the six direct knowledges —
The Buddha’s instruction is done.

With mind well subdued,
The bases of psychic power well developed,
The six direct knowledges are attained —
The Buddha’s instruction is done.

Sensual desires are like swords and spears —
They cut the aggregates to pieces.
What you call the pleasure of life —
For me, that sensual pleasure
Is no longer enticing.

Everywhere, delight is destroyed.
The mass of darkness,
The blinding darkness, has been shattered.
Know this, O Evil One —
You are Māra,
You are defeated.

From: Therīgāthā 11.1
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, these ten perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit, great benefit, merging with the deathless, having the deathless as their end. What…
item.description:
“Monks, these ten perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit, great benefit, merging with the deathless, having the deathless as their end. What ten? The perception of impermanence, the perception of not-self, the perception of death, the perception of disgust with food, the perception of non-delight in the entire world, the perception of a skeleton, the perception of a worm-infested corpse, the perception of a livid corpse, the perception of a fissured corpse, the perception of a bloated corpse. These ten perceptions, monks, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit, great benefit, merging with the deathless, having the deathless as their end.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.57
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, if one does not intend, does not plan but still has a tendency towards something, that becomes a basis for the establishment of consciousness.…
item.description:
“Monks, if one does not intend, does not plan but still has a tendency towards something, that becomes a basis for the establishment of consciousness. When there is a basis, there is an establishment of consciousness. When consciousness is established and grows, there is the descent of name-and-form. With name-and-form as condition, the six sense-bases … such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.39
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Form, sound, taste, smell, touch — All these things Are desirable, delightful, agreeable As long as they exist. The world with its devas Regards them…
item.description:
“Form, sound, taste, smell, touch —
All these things
Are desirable, delightful, agreeable
As long as they exist.

The world with its devas
Regards them as delightful,
But when they cease,
Then they are seen as suffering.

The noble ones see as happiness
The destruction of identity.
This is completely opposite
To what the whole world sees.

What others call happiness,
The noble call suffering.
What others call suffering,
The noble know as happiness.

The good have open eyes, they see, they have light —
Apart from the noble ones,
Who is worthy of perfect enlightenment?
By that right knowledge of the path,
They attain Nibbāna, free from defilements.”

From: Sutta Nipāta 3.12
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Good sirs, what is the cessation of suffering? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, the abandoning and relinquishing of…
item.description:
“Good sirs, what is the cessation of suffering? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, the abandoning and relinquishing of it, freedom from it, non-reliance on it. Good sirs, what is the path leading to the cessation of suffering? It is the Noble Eightfold Path that leads to the cessation of suffering, namely: Right View, Right Intention, Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, Right Concentration.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 9 – Sammādiṭṭhisutta
